text: Can you help me write the handover for whoever takes over the schedule?

Of course. A good handover is short, scannable, and answers the questions someone will have at the worst possible moment. Here's a template you can fill in:

Schedule Handover

1. Where things live
- Where the current schedule is posted and where the master copy is kept
- Login or access details for any scheduling app (share passwords privately, not in the document)
- Where availability requests and time-off requests are collected

2. The weekly rhythm
- When the next schedule needs to be posted
- When availability is due from staff
- Any recurring deadlines, such as payroll cutoffs or supplier orders tied to staffing

3. Rules of thumb
- Minimum number of people needed for each shift
- Who is trained to open and who is trained to close
- Any shifts that are always hard to fill, and what has worked to fill them

4. Open items
- Pending time-off requests and whether they've been approved
- Shift swaps that were agreed but not yet updated
- Anything you promised someone that hasn't happened yet

5. Who to ask
- Who to go to with questions about pay, hiring, or conflicts

Keep it to one or two pages. Print a copy and leave a digital copy wherever the team normally shares things, and walk the next person through it in person if you can. Ten minutes of talking it through saves a lot of confusion later.
And a goodbye message for the team group chat?

Here are two versions, one warm and one shorter.

Version 1 (warm):
"Hi everyone! As most of you know, Friday is my last shift at Lark Café. I wanted to say thank you for making this such a good place to work. I've learned so much from all of you, from handling the morning rush to keeping a sense of humor when the grinder jams. The schedule handover is in the usual spot, and I'll walk whoever is taking it over through it before I go. I'm bringing pastries Friday, so come say hi. Please keep in touch!"

Version 2 (short):
"Hey team, Friday is my last shift. Thank you for everything; I'll miss working with you all. Handover notes are in the usual spot, and there will be pastries. Stay in touch!"

A few tips:
- Post it a few days before your last shift so people who aren't working Friday still see it.
- If there are one or two people who really helped you, a short private message to each of them means more than a mention in the group chat.
- Keep the focus on gratitude rather than on what's next. People will ask, and you can share in person.
I like the first one. Can you make it a bit less formal?

Sure, here's a looser take:

"Hey everyone! Friday's my last shift at Lark Café, which feels really strange to type. Thank you all for being the best crew. You taught me how to survive the morning rush and how to laugh when the grinder jams for the third time in an hour. Handover notes for the schedule are in the usual spot, and I'll go through them in person before I head out. Pastries are on me Friday, so swing by. Don't be strangers!"

If you want it even more casual, you could drop the line about the handover and mention it separately to the person taking over. That keeps the group message purely about saying goodbye.
Now for Fernhill. What should I ask my manager in the first one-on-one?

Your first one-on-one is mostly about understanding expectations and how your manager likes to work. Here's a list to pick from; you won't need all of them in one meeting.

Expectations
- What does a successful first month look like to you? First three months?
- What should I focus on learning first?
- Is there a starter project or a small task I can pick up to learn the process?

How the team works
- How does a project usually flow from brief to shipped design?
- Who are the people I'll work with most closely, outside the design team?
- Which tools and files should I get familiar with first?
- How are design reviews run, and when should I bring work to one?

Working with you
- How often should we meet, and what's the best way to reach you between meetings?
- Do you prefer to see work early and rough, or more polished?
- How do you like to give feedback, and how should I ask for it?

Growth
- What skills do you see as most important for someone in a junior role here?
- Are there people on the team I should learn from?

A tip: bring a notebook or a running doc, and at the end of the meeting repeat back the two or three main things you heard. It shows you were listening and clears up misunderstandings early.
What's a good way to keep that 'things I don't understand yet' list?

Keep it simple enough that you actually use it. Here's a setup that works well:

1. One running document. Use a single note or doc rather than loose sticky notes. Title it something like "Questions and notes."

2. Three sections:
- Questions: anything you don't understand yet. Jargon, acronyms, why a decision was made, how a tool works.
- Answers: when you learn the answer, copy it here with a one-line explanation in your own words. This becomes your personal glossary.
- Observations: things you notice that might be worth raising later, like a confusing flow in the product or a step in the process that seems slow. Don't act on these yet; just collect them.

3. A daily habit. Spend five minutes at the end of each day adding to it and reviewing what's open.

4. Batch your questions. Instead of interrupting people constantly, bring a few questions to your one-on-ones or to your buddy at a set time. Urgent blockers are the exception; ask those right away.

5. Try first, then ask. Before asking, spend ten or fifteen minutes looking in the docs or the design system. When you do ask, say what you already checked. People appreciate it, and you'll often get a better answer.

After a few weeks, the Answers section will be surprisingly long, and it's a nice reminder of how much you've picked up.
Any tips for the user research session if I get to sit in?

Sitting in on research is one of the best ways to learn the product and the users quickly. Some tips:

Before
- Ask the researcher if there's a discussion guide or a list of research questions you can read beforehand.
- Ask what role they'd like you to play: silent observer, note-taker, or occasional question-asker.
- Look at the part of the product being tested so you know what the participant will see.

During
- Stay quiet unless you're invited to speak. Participants get self-conscious with a crowd, and an unplanned question can lead them.
- Write down what people do, not just what they say. Hesitations, wrong clicks, and backtracking are often more telling than opinions.
- Capture direct quotes word for word when something stands out.
- Note the timestamp next to important moments so they're easy to find in the recording.
- Watch your face and body language. Avoid reacting when a participant struggles.

After
- Join the debrief if there is one. Compare notes on the biggest surprises.
- Write down your top three takeaways the same day while they're fresh.
- If something confused you about why the team asked a certain question, add it to your questions list.

One thing to remember: in research, the product is being tested, not the participant. You'll hear that said at the start of most sessions, and it's a useful mindset for reviewing your own work too.
Thanks. Can you put the first-week stuff into a simple checklist?

Here's a checklist you can copy into your notes:

Day 1
[ ] Get laptop, accounts, and tool access working
[ ] Find the design system docs and bookmark them
[ ] Set up the "Questions and notes" document
[ ] Meet your buddy and agree on a regular check-in time

Days 2 to 3
[ ] First one-on-one with your manager (bring your question list)
[ ] Read through recent project briefs or case studies
[ ] Explore the main product as a user would and jot down first impressions
[ ] Learn the file naming and organization conventions for design files

Days 4 to 5
[ ] Ask to sit in on a user research session or design review
[ ] Pick up a small starter task if one is available
[ ] Review your questions list and bring open items to your buddy
[ ] Write a short end-of-week summary: what you learned, what's still unclear, what you'd like to focus on next week

Throughout
[ ] Introduce yourself to the people you'll work with most
[ ] Take notes in meetings and repeat back key points
[ ] Ask for feedback early, even on rough work

The end-of-week summary is optional but useful. Sharing a few lines of it with your manager is an easy way to show progress and get steered in the right direction.
